title: Absolute Entropies and ΔS°
short: ΔS°(reaction) = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants), and the S° of an element is not zero.
trouble: Students set the standard entropy of an element to zero, as they do for ΔH°f.

blocks.html: To put numbers on entropy changes, chemists tabulate standard molar entropies, $S^\circ$. You combine them the way you combined enthalpies of formation, with one important difference.

The third law: a perfect crystal at $0\ \text{K}$ has $S = 0$. So every substance, element or compound, has a positive absolute entropy $S^\circ$ at $298\ \text{K}$. For a reaction, $$\Delta S^\circ = \sum nS^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum nS^\circ(\text{reactants})$$

A perfect crystal at absolute zero has only one possible arrangement: $W = 1$, so $S = k\ln 1 = 0$. That gives entropy a true zero point. Warming a substance from there adds microstates, so $S^\circ$ at $298\ \text{K}$ is measured from heat capacities as an absolute value. Enthalpy has no such zero, which is why $\Delta H^\circ_f$ of an element is defined as zero; $S^\circ$ of an element is not zero at all.

blocks.cap: Standard molar entropies at 298 K. Note the elements: none is zero, and gases are far above solids.

blocks.title: Making ammonia
steps: $\Delta S^\circ = 385.6 - 583.7 = -198.1\ \text{J/K}$. Negative, as expected from 4 mol of gas becoming 2.

blocks.name: ch-microstates
blocks.cap: Why gases have large entropies: on the same lattice, a gas has many more arrangements than a liquid or solid.

blocks.html: Three trends make the table easy to read. Gases have much larger $S^\circ$ than liquids, and liquids than solids. Within one phase, larger and more complex molecules have larger entropies (more ways to vibrate and rotate): $S^\circ$ rises from $\mathrm{CH_4}$ (186.3) to $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ (229.2) to $\mathrm{C_3H_8}$ (270.3). And hard, tightly bonded solids such as diamond (2.4) have very low entropies, while soft solids such as lead (64.8) have higher ones.
Tables of $S^\circ$, $\Delta H^\circ_f$ and $\Delta G^\circ_f$ appear side by side in the back of most textbooks; the values here come from those tables.

Setting the standard entropy of an element to zero, as you do for $\Delta H^\circ_f$. Only a perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy. Check: in the ammonia example, leaving out $\mathrm{N_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2}$ would give $+385.6\ \text{J/K}$, the wrong sign entirely.
See why absolute zero can be approached but never reached in the Science Lab's Absolute Zero and the Third Law chapter.
